                  [0-6658] div
                    [0-6659] separator
                    [0-6661] StaticText: Problems playing these files? See
                    [0-6662] link: media help
                    [0-6664] StaticText: .
                [0-6667] figure
                  [0-6668] span
                    [0-6670] Video: Unable to play media.
                    [0-6782] button: Play video
                    [0-6786] StaticText: Duration: 26 minutes and 21 seconds.
                    [0-6791] StaticText: Subtitles available.
                  [0-6794] link
                  [0-6796] Figcaption
                    [0-6798] StaticText: Complete speech by
                    [0-6799] link: Ronald Reagan
                    [0-6801] StaticText: at the
                    [0-6802] link: Brandenburg Gate
                    [0-6804] StaticText: , 12 June 1987. "Tear down this wall" passage begins at 11:10 into this video.
                [0-6805] paragraph
                  [0-6806] StaticText: On 26 June 1963, 22 months after the erection of the Berlin Wall,
                  [0-6807] link: U.S. President
                  [0-17687] StaticText: 
                  [0-6809] link: John F. Kennedy
                  [0-6811] StaticText: visited West Berlin. Speaking from a platform erected on the steps of
                  [0-6812] link: Rathaus Schöneberg
                  [0-6814] StaticText: for an audience of 450,000 and straying from the prepared script,
                  [0-6815] superscript
                    [0-6816] link: [118]
                      [0-6817] span
                        [0-6819] StaticText: [
                        [0-6820] StaticText: 118
                        [0-6822] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6823] StaticText: he declared in his
                  [0-6825] link: Ich bin ein Berliner
                  [0-6827] StaticText: speech the support of the United States for West Germany and the people of West Berlin in particular:
                [0-6829] blockquote
                  [0-6830] paragraph
                    [0-6831] StaticText: Two thousand years ago, the proudest boast was
                    [0-6833] link: civis Romanus sum
                    [0-6835] StaticText: ["I am a Roman citizen"]. Today, in the world of freedom, the proudest boast is
                    [0-6837] StaticText: "Ich bin ein Berliner!"
                    [0-6838] StaticText: ... All free men, wherever they may live, are citizens of Berlin, and therefore, as a free man, I take pride in the words "Ich bin ein Berliner!"
                [0-6839] paragraph
                  [0-6840] StaticText: The message was aimed as much at the Soviets as it was at Berliners and was a clear statement of U.S. policy in the wake of the construction of the Berlin Wall. The speech is considered one of Kennedy's best, both a significant moment in the
                  [0-6841] link: Cold War
                  [0-6843] StaticText: and a high point of the
                  [0-6844] link: New Frontier
                  [0-6846] StaticText: . It was a great morale boost for West Berliners, who feared a possible East German occupation.
                  [0-6847] superscript
                    [0-6848] link: [119]
                      [0-6849] span
                        [0-6851] StaticText: [
                        [0-6852] StaticText: 119
                        [0-6854] StaticText: ]
                [0-6855] paragraph
                  [0-6856] StaticText: British prime minister
                  [0-6857] link: Margaret Thatcher
                  [0-6859] StaticText: commented in 1982:
                [0-6861] blockquote
                  [0-6862] paragraph
                    [0-6863] StaticText: Every stone bears witness to the moral bankruptcy of the society it encloses.
                    [0-6864] superscript
                      [0-6865] link: [120]
                        [0-6866] span
                          [0-6868] StaticText: [
                          [0-6869] StaticText: 120
                          [0-6871] StaticText: ]
                [0-6872] paragraph
                  [0-6873] StaticText: In
                  [0-6874] link: a speech
                  [0-6876] StaticText: at the
                  [0-6877] link: Brandenburg Gate
                  [0-6879] StaticText: commemorating the 750th anniversary of Berlin
                  [0-6880] superscript
                    [0-6881] link: [121]
                      [0-6882] span
                        [0-6884] StaticText: [
                        [0-6885] StaticText: 121
                        [0-6887] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6888] StaticText: on 12 June 1987, U.S. President
                  [0-6889] link: Ronald Reagan
                  [0-6891] StaticText: challenged
                  [0-6892] link: Mikhail Gorbachev
                  [0-6894] StaticText: , then the
                  [0-6895] link: General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union
                  [0-6897] StaticText: , to tear down the Wall as a symbol of increasing freedom in the
                  [0-6898] link: Eastern Bloc
                  [0-6900] StaticText: :
                [0-6902] blockquote
                  [0-6903] paragraph
                    [0-6904] StaticText: We welcome change and openness; for we believe that freedom and security go together, that the advance of human liberty can only strengthen the cause of world peace. There is one sign the Soviets can make that would be unmistakable, that would advance dramatically the cause of freedom and peace. General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and eastern Europe, if you seek
                    [0-6905] link: liberalization
                    [0-6907] StaticText: , come here to this gate. Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate. Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this Wall!
                    [0-6908] superscript
                      [0-6909] link: [122]
                        [0-6910] span
                          [0-6912] StaticText: [
                          [0-6913] StaticText: 122
                          [0-6915] StaticText: ]
                [0-6916] paragraph
                  [0-6917] StaticText: In January 1989, GDR leader
                  [0-6918] link: Erich Honecker
                  [0-6920] StaticText: predicted that the Wall would stand for 50 or 100 more years
                  [0-6921] superscript
                    [0-6922] link: [123]
                      [0-6923] span
                        [0-6925] StaticText: [
                        [0-6926] StaticText: 123
                        [0-6928] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6929] StaticText: if the conditions that had caused its construction did not change.
              [0-6930] region: Fall
                [0-6932] heading: Fall
                [0-6937] note
                  [0-6938] StaticText: Main article:
                  [0-6939] link: Fall of the Berlin Wall
                [0-6941] paragraph
                  [0-6942] StaticText: Due to the increasing economic problems in the Eastern Bloc and the failure of the USSR to intervene in relation to the individual communist states, the brackets of the Eastern Bloc slowly began to loosen from the end of the 1980s. One example is the fall of the communist government in neighboring
                  [0-6943] link: Poland
                  [0-6945] StaticText: 's
                  [0-6946] link: 1989 Polish parliamentary election
                  [0-6948] StaticText: . Also in June 1989, the Hungarian government began
                  [0-6949] link: dismantling the electrified fence along its border with Austria
                  [0-6951] StaticText: (with Western TV crews present) although the border was still very closely guarded and escape was almost impossible.
                [0-6952] paragraph
                  [0-6953] StaticText: The opening of a border gate between Austria and Hungary at the
                  [0-6954] link: Pan-European Picnic
                  [0-6956] StaticText: on 19 August 1989, which was based on an idea by
                  [0-6957] link: Otto von Habsburg
                  [0-6959] StaticText: to test the reaction of
                  [0-6960] link: Mikhail Gorbachev
                  [0-6962] StaticText: ,
                  [0-6963] superscript
                    [0-6964] link: [124]
                      [0-6965] span
                        [0-6967] StaticText: [
                        [0-6968] StaticText: 124
                        [0-6970] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6971] StaticText: then triggered a peaceful chain reaction, the end of which saw the end of the GDR and the Eastern Bloc. Because of the non-reaction of the USSR and the GDR to the mass exodus, the media-informed Eastern Europeans perceived the decreasing power of their governments, and more and more East Germans were now trying to flee via Hungary. In a comment to the
                  [0-6973] StaticText: Daily Mirror
                  [0-6974] StaticText: regarding the Pan-European Picnic, Erich Honecker showed his people his own inaction: "Habsburg distributed leaflets far into Poland, on which the East German holidaymakers were invited to a picnic. When they came to the picnic, they were given gifts, food and Deutsche Mark, and then they were persuaded to come to the West."
                  [0-6975] superscript
                    [0-6976] link: [14]
                      [0-6977] span
                        [0-6979] StaticText: [
                        [0-6980] StaticText: 14
                        [0-6982] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6983] superscript
                    [0-6984] link: [15]
                      [0-6985] span
                        [0-6987] StaticText: [
                        [0-6988] StaticText: 15
                        [0-6990] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6991] superscript
                    [0-6992] link: [125]
                      [0-6993] span
                        [0-6995] StaticText: [
                        [0-6996] StaticText: 125
                        [0-6998] StaticText: ]
                  [0-6999] StaticText: Then, in September, more than 13,000 East German tourists escaped through
                  [0-7000] link: Hungary
                  [0-7002] StaticText: to
                  [0-7003] link: Austria
                  [0-7005] StaticText: .
                  [0-7006] superscript
                    [0-7007] link: [126]
                      [0-7008] span
                        [0-7010] StaticText: [
                        [0-7011] StaticText: 126
                        [0-7013] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7014] StaticText: This set up a chain of events. The Hungarians prevented many more East Germans from crossing the border and returned them to
                  [0-7015] link: Budapest
                  [0-7017] StaticText: . These East Germans flooded the
                  [0-7018] link: West German embassy
                  [0-7020] StaticText: and refused to return to East Germany.
                  [0-7021] superscript
                    [0-7022] link: [127]
                      [0-7023] span
                        [0-7025] StaticText: [
                        [0-7026] StaticText: 127
                        [0-7028] StaticText: ]
                [0-7029] figure
                  [0-7030] link
                    [0-89] image
                  [0-7032] Figcaption
                    [0-7034] StaticText: East German border guard at Berlin Wall, July 1988
                [0-7035] paragraph
                  [0-7036] StaticText: The East German government responded by disallowing further travel to Hungary but allowed those already there to return to East Germany.
                  [0-7037] superscript
                    [0-7038] link: [128]
                      [0-7039] span
                        [0-7041] StaticText: [
                        [0-7042] StaticText: 128
                        [0-7044] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7045] StaticText: This triggered similar events in neighboring
                  [0-7046] link: Czechoslovakia
                  [0-7048] StaticText: . This time, however, the East German authorities allowed people to leave, provided that they did so by train through East Germany. This was followed by
                  [0-7049] link: mass demonstrations within East Germany itself
                  [0-7051] StaticText: . Protests spread throughout East Germany in September 1989. Initially, protesters were mostly people wanting to leave to the West, chanting
                  [0-7054] StaticText: "Wir wollen raus!"
                  [0-7056] StaticText: ("We want out!"). Then protestors began to chant
                  [0-7059] StaticText: "Wir bleiben hier!"
                  [0-7061] StaticText: ("We are staying here!"). This was the start of what East Germans generally call the "
                  [0-7062] link: Peaceful Revolution
                  [0-7064] StaticText: " of late 1989.
                  [0-7065] superscript
                    [0-7066] link: [129]
                      [0-7067] span
                        [0-7069] StaticText: [
                        [0-7070] StaticText: 129
                        [0-7072] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7073] StaticText: The protest demonstrations grew considerably by early November. The movement neared its height on 4 November, when half a million people gathered to demand political change at the
                  [0-7074] link: Alexanderplatz demonstration
                  [0-7076] StaticText: , in East Berlin's large public square and transportation hub.
                  [0-7077] superscript
                    [0-7078] link: [130]
                      [0-7079] span
                        [0-7081] StaticText: [
                        [0-7082] StaticText: 130
                        [0-7084] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7085] StaticText: On 9 October 1989, the police and army units were given permission to use force against those assembled, but this did not deter the church service and march from taking place, which gathered 70,000 people.
                  [0-7086] superscript
                    [0-7087] link: [131]
                      [0-7088] span
                        [0-7090] StaticText: [
                        [0-7091] StaticText: 131
                        [0-7093] StaticText: ]
                [0-7094] paragraph
                  [0-7095] StaticText: The longtime leader of East Germany,
                  [0-7096] link: Erich Honecker
                  [0-7098] StaticText: , resigned on 18 October 1989 and was replaced by
                  [0-7099] link: Egon Krenz
                  [0-7101] StaticText: that day.
                [0-7102] paragraph
                  [0-7103] StaticText: The wave of refugees leaving East Germany for the West kept increasing. By early November refugees were finding their way to Hungary via Czechoslovakia, or via the
                  [0-7104] link: West German embassy in Prague
                  [0-7106] StaticText: . This was tolerated by the new Krenz government, because of long-standing agreements with the communist Czechoslovak government, allowing free travel across their common border. However, this movement of people grew so large it caused difficulties for both countries. To ease the difficulties, the politburo led by Krenz decided on 9 November to allow refugees to exit directly through crossing points between East Germany and West Germany, including between East and West Berlin. Later the same day, the ministerial administration modified the proposal to include private, round-trip, and travel. The new regulations were to take effect the next day.
                  [0-7107] superscript
                    [0-7108] link: [132]
                      [0-7109] span
                        [0-7111] StaticText: [
                        [0-7112] StaticText: 132
                        [0-7114] StaticText: ]
                [0-7115] figure
                  [0-7116] link
                    [0-78] image
                  [0-7118] Figcaption
                    [0-7120] StaticText: East German military parade in
                    [0-7121] link: Karl-Marx-Allee
                    [0-7123] StaticText: ,
                    [0-7124] link: East Berlin
                    [0-7126] StaticText: in August 1986, celebrating the "25th anniversary of the Anti-Fascist Protection Wall", the official name of the Berlin Wall
                [0-7127] paragraph
                  [0-7128] link: Günter Schabowski
                  [0-7130] StaticText: , the party boss in East Berlin and the spokesman for the SED Politburo, had the task of announcing the new regulations. However, he had not been involved in the discussions about the new regulations and had not been fully updated.
                  [0-7131] superscript
                    [0-7132] link: [133]
                      [0-7133] span
                        [0-7135] StaticText: [
                        [0-7136] StaticText: 133
                        [0-7138] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7139] StaticText: Shortly before a press conference on 9 November, he was handed a note announcing the changes, but given no further instructions on how to handle the information. These regulations had only been completed a few hours earlier and were to take effect the following day, so as to allow time to inform the border guards. But this starting time delay was not communicated to Schabowski.
                  [0-7140] superscript
                    [0-7141] link: [56]
                      [0-7142] span
                        [0-7144] StaticText: [
                        [0-7145] StaticText: 56
                        [0-7147] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7149] superscript
                    [0-7151] StaticText: [
                    [0-7153] link: page needed
                      [0-7154] span
                        [0-7155] StaticText: page
                        [0-7157] StaticText: 
                        [0-7158] StaticText: needed
                    [0-7160] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7161] StaticText: At the end of the press conference, Schabowski read out loud the note he had been given. A reporter,
                  [0-7162] link: ANSA
                  [0-7164] StaticText: 's
                  [0-7165] link: Riccardo Ehrman
                  [0-7167] StaticText: ,
                  [0-7168] superscript
                    [0-7169] link: [134]
                      [0-7170] span
                        [0-7172] StaticText: [
                        [0-7173] StaticText: 134
                        [0-7175] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7176] StaticText: asked when the regulations would take effect. After a few seconds' hesitation, Schabowski replied, "As far as I know, it takes effect immediately, without delay".
                  [0-7177] superscript
                    [0-7178] link: [56]
                      [0-7179] span
                        [0-7181] StaticText: [
                        [0-7182] StaticText: 56
                        [0-7184] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7186] superscript
                    [0-7188] StaticText: [
                    [0-7190] link: page needed
                      [0-7191] span
                        [0-7192] StaticText: page
                        [0-7194] StaticText: 
                        [0-7195] StaticText: needed
                    [0-7197] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7198] StaticText: After further questions from journalists, he confirmed that the regulations included the border crossings through the Wall into West Berlin, which he had not mentioned until then.
                  [0-7199] superscript
                    [0-7200] link: [135]
                      [0-7201] span
                        [0-7203] StaticText: [
                        [0-7204] StaticText: 135
                        [0-7206] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7207] StaticText: He repeated that it was immediate in an interview with American journalist
                  [0-7208] link: Tom Brokaw
                  [0-7210] StaticText: .
                  [0-7211] superscript
                    [0-111] link: [136]
                      [0-7212] span
                        [0-7214] StaticText: [
                        [0-7215] StaticText: 136
                        [0-7217] StaticText: ]
                [0-7218] paragraph
                  [0-7219] StaticText: Excerpts from Schabowski's press conference were the lead story on West Germany's two main news programs that night—at 7:17
                  [0-7221] StaticText: 
                  [0-7222] StaticText: p.m. on
                  [0-7223] link: ZDF
                  [0-7225] StaticText: 's
                  [0-7227] link: heute
                  [0-7229] StaticText: and at 8 p.m. on
                  [0-7230] link: ARD
                  [0-7232] StaticText: 's
                  [0-7234] StaticText: Tagesschau
                  [0-7235] StaticText: . As ARD and ZDF had broadcast to
                  [0-7236] link: nearly all of East Germany
                  [0-7238] StaticText: since the late 1950s and had become accepted by the East German authorities, the news was broadcast there as well simultaneously. Later that night, on ARD's
                  [0-7240] link: Tagesthemen
                  [0-7242] StaticText: , anchorman
                  [0-7243] link: Hanns Joachim Friedrichs
                  [0-7245] StaticText: proclaimed, "This 9 November is a historic day. The GDR has announced that, starting immediately, its borders are open to everyone. The gates in the Wall stand open wide."
                  [0-7246] superscript
                    [0-7247] link: [56]
                      [0-7248] span
                        [0-7250] StaticText: [
                        [0-7251] StaticText: 56
                        [0-7253] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7255] superscript
                    [0-7257] StaticText: [
                    [0-7259] link: page needed
                      [0-7260] span
                        [0-7261] StaticText: page
                        [0-7263] StaticText: 
                        [0-7264] StaticText: needed
                    [0-7266] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7267] superscript
                    [0-7268] link: [133]
                      [0-7269] span
                        [0-7271] StaticText: [
                        [0-7272] StaticText: 133
                        [0-7274] StaticText: ]
                [0-7275] paragraph
                  [0-7276] StaticText: After hearing the broadcast, East Germans began gathering at the Wall, at the six checkpoints between East and West Berlin, demanding that border guards immediately open the gates.
                  [0-7277] superscript
                    [0-7278] link: [133]
                      [0-7279] span
                        [0-7281] StaticText: [
                        [0-7282] StaticText: 133
                        [0-7284] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7285] StaticText: The surprised and overwhelmed guards made many hectic telephone calls to their superiors about the problem. At first, they were ordered to find the "more aggressive" people gathered at the gates and stamp their passports with a special stamp that barred them from returning to East Germany—in effect, revoking their citizenship. However, this still left thousands of people demanding to be let through "as Schabowski said we can".
                  [0-7286] superscript
                    [0-7287] link: [56]
                      [0-7288] span
                        [0-7290] StaticText: [
                        [0-7291] StaticText: 56
                        [0-7293] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7295] superscript
                    [0-7297] StaticText: [
                    [0-7299] link: page needed
                      [0-7300] span
                        [0-7301] StaticText: page
                        [0-7303] StaticText: 
                        [0-7304] StaticText: needed
                    [0-7306] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7307] StaticText: It soon became clear that no one among the East German authorities would take personal responsibility for issuing orders to use lethal force, so the vastly outnumbered soldiers had no way to hold back the huge crowd of East German citizens. Finally, at 10:45
                  [0-7309] StaticText: 
                  [0-7310] StaticText: p.m. on 9 November,
                  [0-7311] link: Harald Jäger
                  [0-7313] StaticText: , the commander of the
                  [0-7314] link: Bornholmer Straße border crossing
                  [0-7316] StaticText: yielded, allowing the guards to open the checkpoints and allowing people through with little or no identity checking.
                  [0-7317] superscript
                    [0-7318] link: [137]
                      [0-7319] span
                        [0-7321] StaticText: [
                        [0-7322] StaticText: 137
                        [0-7324] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7325] StaticText: As the
                  [0-7327] link: Ossis
                  [0-7329] StaticText: swarmed through, they were greeted by
                  [0-7331] link: Wessis
                  [0-7333] StaticText: waiting with flowers and champagne amid wild rejoicing. Soon afterward, a crowd of West Berliners jumped on top of the Wall, and were soon joined by East German youngsters.
                  [0-7334] superscript
                    [0-7335] link: [138]
                      [0-7336] span
                        [0-7338] StaticText: [
                        [0-7339] StaticText: 138
                        [0-7341] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7342] StaticText: The evening of 9 November 1989 is known as the night the Wall came down.
                  [0-7343] superscript
                    [0-7344] link: [139]
                      [0-7345] span
                        [0-7347] StaticText: [
                        [0-7348] StaticText: 139
                        [0-7350] StaticText: ]
                [0-7351] paragraph
                  [0-7352] StaticText: Another border crossing to the south may have been opened earlier. An account by
                  [0-7353] link: Heinz Schäfer
                  [0-7355] StaticText: indicates that he also acted independently and ordered the opening of the gate at Waltersdorf-Rudow a couple of hours earlier.
                  [0-7356] superscript
                    [0-7357] link: [140]
                      [0-7358] span
                        [0-7360] StaticText: [
                        [0-7361] StaticText: 140
                        [0-7363] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7364] StaticText: This may explain reports of East Berliners appearing in West Berlin earlier than the opening of the Bornholmer Straße border crossing.
                  [0-7365] superscript
                    [0-7366] link: [141]
                      [0-7367] span
                        [0-7369] StaticText: [
                        [0-7370] StaticText: 141
                        [0-7372] StaticText: ]
                [0-7373] paragraph
                  [0-7374] StaticText: Thirty years after the fall of the Berlin Wall,
                  [0-7376] link: The Guardian
                  [0-7378] StaticText: collected short stories from 9 November 1989 by five German writers who reflect on the day. In this,
                  [0-7379] link: Kathrin Schmidt
                  [0-7381] StaticText: remembers comically: "I downed almost an entire bottle of schnapps".
                  [0-7382] superscript
                    [0-7383] link: [142]
                      [0-7384] span
                        [0-7386] StaticText: [
                        [0-7387] StaticText: 142
                        [0-7389] StaticText: ]

                  [0-7468] listitem
                    [0-7471] link: A hole in the Berlin wall, 2019

                [0-7475] figure
                  [0-7476] link
                    [0-90] image
                  [0-7478] Figcaption
                    [0-7480] StaticText: Remaining stretch of the Wall near
                    [0-7481] link: Ostbahnhof
                    [0-7483] StaticText: in
                    [0-7484] link: Friedrichshain
                    [0-7486] StaticText: called
                    [0-7487] link: East Side Gallery
                    [0-7489] StaticText: , August 2006
                [0-7490] paragraph
                  [0-7491] StaticText: Little is left of the Wall at its original site, which was destroyed almost in its entirety. Three long sections are still standing: an
                  [0-7493] StaticText: 80-metre-long (260
                  [0-7495] StaticText: 
                  [0-7497] StaticText: ft)
                  [0-7498] StaticText: piece of the first (westernmost) wall at the
                  [0-7499] link: Topography of Terror
                  [0-7501] StaticText: , site of the former
                  [0-7502] link: Gestapo
                  [0-7504] StaticText: headquarters, halfway between Checkpoint Charlie and
                  [0-7505] link: Potsdamer Platz
                  [0-7507] StaticText: ; a longer section of the second (easternmost) wall along the
                  [0-7508] link: Spree
                  [0-7510] StaticText: River near the
                  [0-7513] link: Oberbaumbrücke
                  [0-7516] StaticText: , nicknamed
                  [0-7517] link: East Side Gallery
                  [0-7519] StaticText: ; and a third section that is partly reconstructed, in the north at Bernauer Straße, which was turned into a memorial in 1998. Other isolated fragments, lampposts, other elements, and a few watchtowers also remain in various parts of the city.
                [0-7520] list
                  [0-7521] listitem
                    [0-7522] ListMarker: •
                    [0-7523] StaticText: The former leadership in the Schlesischen Busch in the vicinity of the Puschkinallee—the listed, twelve-meter high watchtower stands in a piece of the wall strip, which has been turned into a park, near the
                    [0-7524] link: Lohmühleninsel
                    [0-7526] StaticText: .
                    [0-7527] superscript

                  [0-7535] listitem
                    [0-7536] ListMarker: •
                    [0-7537] StaticText: The former "Kieler Eck" (
                    [0-7538] link: Kiel
                    [0-7540] StaticText: Corner) on Kieler Strasse in
                    [0-7541] link: Mitte
                    [0-7543] StaticText: , close to the Berlin-Spandau Schifffahrtskanal—the tower is protected as a historic monument and now surrounded on three sides by new buildings. It houses a memorial site named after the Wallopfer
                    [0-7544] link: Günter Litfin
                    [0-7546] StaticText: , who was shot at
                    [0-7547] link: Humboldthafen
                    [0-7549] StaticText: in August 1961. The memorial site, which is run by the initiative of his brother Jürgen Liftin, can be viewed after registration.
                  [0-7550] listitem
                    [0-7551] ListMarker: •
                    [0-7552] StaticText: The former management office at Nieder Neuendorf, in the district of
                    [0-7553] link: Hennigsdorf
                    [0-7555] StaticText: of the same name—here is the permanent exhibition on the history of the border installations between the two German states.
                  [0-7556] listitem
                    [0-7557] ListMarker: •
                    [0-7558] StaticText: The former management station at Bergfelde, today the district of
                    [0-7559] link: Hohen Neuendorf
                    [0-7561] StaticText: —The tower is located in an already reforested area of the border strip and is used together with surrounding terrain as a nature protection tower by the Deutschen Waldjugend.
                  [0-7562] listitem
                    [0-7563] ListMarker: •
                    [0-7564] StaticText: The only one of the much slimmer observation towers (BT-11) in the Erna-Berger-Strasse also in Mitte—however, was moved by a few meters for construction work and is no longer in the original location; There is an exhibition about the wall in the area of the Potsdamer Platz in planning.
                [0-7565] figure
                  [0-7566] link
                    [0-72] image
                  [0-7568] Figcaption
                    [0-7570] StaticText: Line indicating where the inner part of the wall once stood on
                    [0-7571] link: Leipziger Platz
                    [0-7573] StaticText: , just off
                    [0-7574] link: Potsdamer Platz
                    [0-7576] StaticText: , in 2015
                [0-7577] paragraph
                  [0-7578] StaticText: Nothing still accurately represents the Wall's original appearance better than a very short stretch at Bernauer Straße associated with the Berlin Wall Documentation Center.
                  [0-7579] superscript
                    [0-7580] link: [144]
                      [0-7581] span
                        [0-7583] StaticText: [
                        [0-7584] StaticText: 144
                        [0-7586] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7587] StaticText: Other remnants are badly damaged by souvenir seekers. Fragments of the Wall were taken, and some were sold around the world. Appearing both with and without
                  [0-7588] link: certificates of authenticity
                  [0-7590] StaticText: , these fragments are now a staple on the online auction service
                  [0-7591] link: eBay
                  [0-7593] StaticText: as well as German souvenir shops. Today, the eastern side is covered in
                  [0-7594] link: graffiti
                  [0-7596] StaticText: that did not exist while the Wall was guarded by the armed soldiers of East Germany. Previously, graffiti appeared only on the western side. Along some tourist areas of the city centre, the city government has marked the location of the former Wall by a row of cobblestones in the street. In most places only the "first" wall is marked, except near Potsdamer Platz where the stretch of both walls is marked, giving visitors an impression of the dimension of the barrier system.
                [0-7597] paragraph
                  [0-7598] StaticText: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, there were initiatives that they want to preserve the death strip walkways and redevelop them into a hiking and cycling area, known as
                  [0-7602] StaticText: Berliner Mauerweg
                  [0-7604] StaticText: . It is part of the initiative by the Berlin Senate since 11 October 2001.
                  [0-7605] superscript
                    [0-7606] link: [145]
                      [0-7607] span

                        [0-7612] StaticText: ]
                [0-7613] region: Cultural differences
                  [0-7615] heading: Cultural differences
                  [0-7617] figure
                    [0-7618] link
                      [0-86] image
                    [0-7620] Figcaption
                      [0-7622] StaticText: Remains of the Berlin wall, 2016
                  [0-7623] figure
                    [0-7624] link
                      [0-81] image
                    [0-7626] Figcaption
                      [0-7628] StaticText: Segment of the Berlin wall in the
                      [0-7629] link: Sanctuary of Fátima
                      [0-7631] StaticText: ,
                      [0-7632] link: Portugal
                  [0-7634] paragraph
                    [0-7635] StaticText: For many years after reunification, people in Germany talked about cultural differences between East and West Germans (colloquially
                    [0-7636] link: Ossis and Wessis
                      [0-7638] StaticText: Ossis
                      [0-7639] StaticText: and
                      [0-7641] StaticText: Wessis
                    [0-7642] StaticText: ), sometimes described as
                    [0-7644] StaticText: Mauer im Kopf
                    [0-7645] StaticText: (The wall in the head). A September 2004 poll found that 25 percent of West Germans and 12 percent of East Germans wished that East and West should be separated again by a "Wall".
                    [0-7646] superscript
                      [0-7647] link: [146]
                        [0-7648] span
                          [0-7650] StaticText: [
                          [0-7651] StaticText: 146
                          [0-7653] StaticText: ]
                    [0-7654] StaticText: A poll taken in October 2009 on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of the fall of the Wall indicated, however, that only about a tenth of the population was still unhappy with the unification (8 percent in the East; 12 percent in the West). Although differences are still perceived between East and West, Germans make similar distinctions between
                    [0-7655] link: North
                    [0-7657] StaticText: and
                    [0-7658] link: South
                    [0-7660] StaticText: .
                    [0-7661] superscript
                      [0-7662] link: [147]
                        [0-7663] span
                          [0-7665] StaticText: [
                          [0-7666] StaticText: 147
                          [0-7668] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7669] paragraph
                    [0-7670] StaticText: A 2009 poll conducted by Russia's VTsIOM, found that more than half of all Russians do not know who built the Berlin Wall. Ten percent of people surveyed thought Berlin residents built it themselves. Six percent said Western powers built it and four percent thought it was a "bilateral initiative" of the
                    [0-7671] link: Soviet Union
                    [0-7673] StaticText: and the West. Fifty-eight percent said they did not know who built it, with just 24 percent correctly naming the Soviet Union and its then-communist ally East Germany.
                    [0-7674] superscript
                      [0-7675] link: [148]
                        [0-7676] span
                          [0-7678] StaticText: [
                          [0-7679] StaticText: 148
                          [0-7681] StaticText: ]
                [0-7682] region: Wall segments around the world
                  [0-7684] heading: Wall segments around the world
                  [0-7688] note
                    [0-7689] StaticText: Main article:
                    [0-7690] link: List of Berlin Wall segments
                  [0-7692] paragraph
                    [0-7693] StaticText: Not all segments of the Wall were ground up as the Wall was being torn down. Many segments have been given to various institutions around the world. They can be found, for instance, in presidential and historical museums, lobbies of hotels and corporations, at universities and government buildings, and in public spaces in different countries of the world.
                    [0-7694] superscript
                      [0-7695] link: [149]
                        [0-7696] span
                          [0-7698] StaticText: [
                          [0-7699] StaticText: 149
                          [0-7701] StaticText: ]
                [0-7702] region: 50th anniversary commemoration
                  [0-7704] heading: 50th anniversary commemoration
                  [0-7706] paragraph
                    [0-7707] StaticText: On 13 August 2011, Germany marked the 50th anniversary of East Germany beginning the erection of the Berlin Wall. Chancellor
                    [0-7708] link: Angela Merkel
                    [0-7710] StaticText: joined with President
                    [0-7711] link: Christian Wulff
                    [0-7713] StaticText: and Berlin Mayor
                    [0-7714] link: Klaus Wowereit
                    [0-7716] StaticText: at the Bernauer Straße memorial park to remember lives and liberty. Speeches extolled freedom and a minute of silence at noon honored those who died trying to flee to the West. "It is our shared responsibility to keep the memory alive and to pass it on to the coming generations as a reminder to stand up for freedom and democracy to ensure that such injustice may never happen again." entreated Mayor Wowereit. "It has been shown once again: Freedom is invincible at the end. No wall can permanently withstand the desire for freedom", proclaimed President Wulff.

                [0-7754] region: Polling
                  [0-7756] heading: Polling
                  [0-7758] paragraph
                    [0-7759] StaticText: A small minority still support the wall or even support rebuilding the wall back up. In 2008 a poll found that 11% of participants from the former West Berlin and 12% from the former East Berlin said it would be better if the wall was still in place.
                    [0-7760] superscript
                      [0-7761] link: [154]
                        [0-7762] span
                          [0-7764] StaticText: [
                          [0-7765] StaticText: 154
                          [0-7767] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7768] paragraph
                    [0-7769] StaticText: A November 2009 poll found that 12% of Germans said the wall should be rebuilt. The poll also found that in the former
                    [0-7770] link: West German states
                    [0-7772] StaticText: support was at 12% and in the former
                    [0-7773] link: East German states
                    [0-7775] StaticText: it was 13%. A September 2009 poll found 15% of Germans supported a wall, while in the west it was 16% and in the east it was at 10%.
                    [0-7776] superscript
                      [0-7777] link: [155]
                        [0-7778] span

                  [0-7792] paragraph
                    [0-7793] StaticText: A 2010 poll from Emnid for
                    [0-7795] link: Bild
                    [0-7797] StaticText: , found that 24% of West Germans and 23% of East Germans wished for the wall still being in place.
                    [0-7798] superscript

                  [0-7830] paragraph
                    [0-7831] StaticText: A 2011 poll from
                    [0-7832] link: Forsa
                    [0-7834] StaticText: found 35% of Berliners thought the construction of the Wall was not so wrong with supporters of
                    [0-7835] link: the Left Party
                    [0-7837] StaticText: at 74%.
                    [0-7838] superscript
                      [0-7839] link: [161]
                        [0-7840] span
                          [0-7842] StaticText: [

                          [0-7845] StaticText: ]
                  [0-7846] paragraph
                    [0-7847] StaticText: A 2019 poll from
                    [0-7849] link: Berliner Zeitung
                    [0-7851] StaticText: on the 30th anniversary, found that 8% of Berliners supported the idea if the wall was still standing, and the overwhelming majority of Berliners at 87% supported the fall of the wall. The poll also found that 28% of the
                    [0-7852] link: Alternative for Germany
                    [0-7854] StaticText: (AfD) and 16% of
                    [0-7855] link: Free Democratic Party
                    [0-7857] StaticText: (FDP) supporters supported bringing back the wall.
                    [0-7858] superscript
                      [0-7859] link: [162]
                        [0-7860] span
                          [0-7862] StaticText: [
                          [0-7863] StaticText: 162
                          [0-7865] StaticText: ]
                    [0-7866] StaticText: A 2019
                    [0-7867] link: Yougov
                    [0-7869] StaticText: poll found that 13% of Germans wanted the wall back, in the West support was at 14% and in the East it was 13%.

                        [0-23807] link: Great Britain
                        [0-17969] StaticText: .

                        [0-17971] StaticText: was prime minister during much of the

                        [0-17973] StaticText: .
                  [0-23816] div

                      [0-23822] div
                        [0-23823] link: Margaret Thatcher
                        [0-17975] StaticText: was the first female prime minister.
                    [0-23824] div
                      [0-23827] link
                        [0-23828] image
                      [0-23829] div
                        [0-23830] link: Andy Burnham
                        [0-17977] StaticText: is the current prime minister.
                [0-23833] paragraph
                  [0-17978] StaticText: The
                  [0-23834] link: prime minister of the United Kingdom
                  [0-17980] StaticText: is the principal
                  [0-23835] link: minister of the Crown
                  [0-17982] StaticText: of
                  [0-23836] link: His Majesty's Government
                  [0-17984] StaticText: , and the head of the
                  [0-23837] link: British Cabinet
                  [0-17986] StaticText: .
                [0-23838] paragraph
                  [0-17987] StaticText: There is no specific date for when the office of prime minister first appeared, as the role was not created but rather evolved over time through a merger of duties.
                  [0-23839] superscript
                    [0-23840] link: [1]
                      [0-23841] span
                        [0-17988] StaticText: [
                        [0-17989] StaticText: 1
                        [0-17990] StaticText: ]
                  [0-17991] StaticText: The term was regularly, if informally, used by
                  [0-23844] link: Robert Walpole
                  [0-17993] StaticText: by the 1730s.
                  [0-23845] superscript
                    [0-23846] link: [2]
                      [0-23847] span
                        [0-17994] StaticText: [
                        [0-17995] StaticText: 2
                        [0-17996] StaticText: ]
                  [0-17997] StaticText: It was used in the
                  [0-23850] link: House of Commons
                  [0-17999] StaticText: as early as 1805,
                  [0-23851] superscript
                    [0-23852] link: [3]
                      [0-23853] span
                        [0-18000] StaticText: [
                        [0-18001] StaticText: 3
                        [0-18002] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18003] StaticText: and it was certainly in parliamentary use by the 1880s,
                  [0-23856] superscript
                    [0-23857] link: [4]
                      [0-23858] span
                        [0-18004] StaticText: [
                        [0-18005] StaticText: 4
                        [0-18006] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18007] StaticText: but did not become the official title until 1905, when
                  [0-23861] link: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
                  [0-18009] StaticText: was prime minister.
                [0-23862] paragraph
                  [0-18010] StaticText: Historians generally consider
                  [0-23863] link: Robert Walpole
                  [0-18012] StaticText: , who led the government of the
                  [0-23864] link: Kingdom of Great Britain
                  [0-18014] StaticText: for over twenty years from 1721,
                  [0-23865] superscript
                    [0-23866] link: [5]
                      [0-23867] span
                        [0-18015] StaticText: [
                        [0-18016] StaticText: 5
                        [0-18017] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18018] StaticText: to be the first prime minister. Walpole is also the longest-serving British prime minister by this definition.
                  [0-23870] superscript
                    [0-23871] link: [6]
                      [0-23872] span
                        [0-18019] StaticText: [
                        [0-18020] StaticText: 6
                        [0-18021] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18022] StaticText: The first prime minister of the
                  [0-23875] link: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
                  [0-18024] StaticText: was
                  [0-23876] link: William Pitt the Younger
                  [0-18026] StaticText: at its creation on 1 January 1801.
                  [0-23877] superscript
                    [0-23878] link: [7]
                      [0-23879] span
                        [0-18027] StaticText: [
                        [0-18028] StaticText: 7
                        [0-18029] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18030] StaticText: The first to use the title in an official act was
                  [0-23882] link: Benjamin Disraeli
                  [0-18032] StaticText: who signed the
                  [0-23883] link: 1878 Treaty of Berlin
                  [0-18034] StaticText: as "Prime Minister of Her Britannic Majesty".
                  [0-23884] superscript
                    [0-23885] link: [8]
                      [0-23886] span
                        [0-18035] StaticText: [
                        [0-18036] StaticText: 8
                        [0-18037] StaticText: ]
                [0-23889] paragraph
                  [0-18038] StaticText: In 1905, the post of prime minister was officially given recognition in the
                  [0-23890] link: order of precedence
                  [0-18040] StaticText: ,
                  [0-23891] superscript
                    [0-23892] link: [9]
                      [0-23893] span
                        [0-18041] StaticText: [
                        [0-18042] StaticText: 9
                        [0-18043] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18044] StaticText: with the incumbent
                  [0-23896] link: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
                  [0-18046] StaticText: the first officially referred to as "prime minister". The first prime minister of the current
                  [0-23897] link: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
                  [0-18048] StaticText: upon its creation in 1922 (when 26 Irish counties seceded and created the
                  [0-23898] link: Irish Free State
                  [0-18050] StaticText: ) was
                  [0-23899] link: Andrew Bonar Law
                  [0-18052] StaticText: ,
                  [0-23900] superscript
                    [0-23901] link: [10]
                      [0-23902] span
                        [0-18053] StaticText: [
                        [0-18054] StaticText: 10
                        [0-18055] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18056] StaticText: although the country was not renamed officially until 1927, when
                  [0-23905] link: Stanley Baldwin
                  [0-18058] StaticText: was the serving prime minister.
                  [0-23906] superscript
                    [0-23907] link: [11]
                      [0-23908] span

                    [0-23925] link: edit
                  [0-23928] paragraph
                    [0-18070] StaticText: Before the
                    [0-23929] link: Union of England and Scotland
                    [0-18072] StaticText: in 1707, the
                    [0-23930] link: Treasury
                    [0-18074] StaticText: of
                    [0-23931] link: England
                    [0-18076] StaticText: was led by the
                    [0-23932] link: Lord High Treasurer
                    [0-18078] StaticText: .
                    [0-23933] superscript
                      [0-23934] link: [12]
                        [0-23935] span
                          [0-18079] StaticText: [
                          [0-18080] StaticText: 12
                          [0-18081] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18082] StaticText: By the late
                    [0-23938] link: Tudor period
                    [0-18084] StaticText: , the Lord High Treasurer was regarded as one of the
                    [0-23939] link: Great Officers of State
                    [0-18086] StaticText: ,
                    [0-23940] superscript
                      [0-23941] link: [12]
                        [0-23942] span
                          [0-18087] StaticText: [
                          [0-18088] StaticText: 12
                          [0-18089] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18090] StaticText: and was often (though not always) the dominant figure in government:
                    [0-23945] link: Edward Seymour, 1st Duke of Somerset
                    [0-18092] StaticText: (lord high treasurer, 1547–1549),
                    [0-23946] superscript
                      [0-23947] link: [13]
                        [0-23948] span
                          [0-18093] StaticText: [
                          [0-18094] StaticText: 13
                          [0-18095] StaticText: ]

                    [0-23951] link: lord protector
                    [0-18098] StaticText: to his young nephew King
                    [0-23952] link: Edward VI
                    [0-18100] StaticText: ;
                    [0-23953] superscript
                      [0-23954] link: [13]

                          [0-18103] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18104] StaticText: 
                    [0-23958] link: William Cecil, 1st Baron Burghley
                    [0-18106] StaticText: (lord high treasurer, 1572–1598),
                    [0-23959] superscript
                      [0-23960] link: [14]
                        [0-23961] span
                          [0-18107] StaticText: [
                          [0-18108] StaticText: 14
                          [0-18109] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18110] StaticText: was the
                    [0-23964] link: dominant minister
                    [0-18112] StaticText: to Queen
                    [0-23965] link: Elizabeth I
                    [0-18114] StaticText: ;
                    [0-23966] superscript
                      [0-23967] link: [14]
                        [0-23968] span
                          [0-18115] StaticText: [
                          [0-18116] StaticText: 14
                          [0-18117] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18118] StaticText: Burghley's son
                    [0-23971] link: Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury
                    [0-18120] StaticText: , succeeded his father as
                    [0-23972] link: chief minister
                    [0-18122] StaticText: to Elizabeth (1598–1603) and was eventually appointed by King
                    [0-23973] link: James I
                      [0-18123] StaticText: James
                      [0-18124] StaticText: 
                      [0-18125] StaticText: I
                    [0-18126] StaticText: as lord high treasurer (1608–1612).
                    [0-23975] superscript
                      [0-23976] link: [15]
                        [0-23977] span
                          [0-18127] StaticText: [
                          [0-18128] StaticText: 15
                          [0-18129] StaticText: ]
                  [0-23980] paragraph
                    [0-18130] StaticText: By the late
                    [0-23981] link: Stuart period
                    [0-18132] StaticText: , the Treasury was often run not by a single individual (i.e., the lord high treasurer) but by a
                    [0-23982] link: commission
                    [0-18134] StaticText: of
                    [0-23983] link: lords of the Treasury

                    [0-23984] superscript
                      [0-23985] link: [16]
                        [0-23986] span
                          [0-18137] StaticText: [
                          [0-18138] StaticText: 16
                          [0-18139] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18140] StaticText: led by the
                    [0-23989] link: first lord of the Treasury
                    [0-18142] StaticText: . The last lords high treasurer,
                    [0-23990] link: Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin

                          [0-18148] StaticText: 17
                          [0-18149] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18150] StaticText: ran the government of
                    [0-23997] link: Queen Anne
                    [0-18152] StaticText: .
                    [0-23998] superscript
                      [0-23999] link: [18]
                        [0-24000] span

                [0-24003] region: Kingdom of Scotland

                  [0-24011] paragraph
                    [0-18160] StaticText: The
                    [0-24012] link: Chancellor of Scotland
                    [0-18162] StaticText: was effectively the first minister of the kingdom. His department, the
                    [0-24013] link: chancery
                    [0-18164] StaticText: , was responsible for the
                    [0-24014] link: Great Seal

                    [0-24015] link: privy council

                    [0-24016] link: court of session

                      [0-24018] link: [19]
                        [0-24019] span

                          [0-18172] StaticText: 19
                          [0-18173] StaticText: ]
                    [0-18174] StaticText: The last Chancellor of Scotland, who ran the government during Queen Anne's reign, was
                    [0-24022] link: James Ogilvy, 1st Earl of Seafield
                    [0-18176] StaticText: .
              [0-24023] region: From 1707 to 1721
                [0-24024] div

                  [0-24028] link: edit
                [0-24031] paragraph
                  [0-18181] StaticText: Following the succession of
                  [0-19555] link: George I
                    [0-18182] StaticText: George
                    [0-18183] StaticText: 
                    [0-18184] StaticText: I
                  [0-18185] StaticText: in 1714, the arrangement of a commission of lords of the Treasury (as opposed to a single lord high treasurer) became permanent.
                  [0-24033] superscript
                    [0-24034] link: [20]
                      [0-24035] span
                        [0-18186] StaticText: [
                        [0-18187] StaticText: 20
                        [0-18188] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18189] StaticText: For the next three years, the government was headed by
                  [0-24038] link: Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend
                  [0-18191] StaticText: , who was appointed
                  [0-24039] link: Secretary of State for the Northern Department
                  [0-18193] StaticText: .
                  [0-24040] superscript
                    [0-24041] link: [21]
                      [0-24042] span
                        [0-18194] StaticText: [
                        [0-18195] StaticText: 21
                        [0-18196] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18197] StaticText: Subsequently, Lords
                  [0-24045] link: Stanhope
                  [0-18199] StaticText: and
                  [0-24046] link: Sunderland
                  [0-18201] StaticText: ran the government jointly,
                  [0-24047] superscript
                    [0-24048] link: [22]
                      [0-24049] span
                        [0-18202] StaticText: [
                        [0-18203] StaticText: 22
                        [0-18204] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18205] StaticText: with Stanhope managing foreign affairs and Sunderland domestic.
                  [0-24052] superscript
                    [0-24053] link: [22]
                      [0-24054] span
                        [0-18206] StaticText: [
                        [0-18207] StaticText: 22
                        [0-18208] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18209] StaticText: Stanhope died in February 1721 and Sunderland resigned two months later;
                  [0-24057] superscript
                    [0-24058] link: [22]
                      [0-24059] span
                        [0-18210] StaticText: [
                        [0-18211] StaticText: 22
                        [0-18212] StaticText: ]

                  [0-24063] superscript
                    [0-24064] link: [23]
                      [0-24065] span
                        [0-18216] StaticText: [
                        [0-18217] StaticText: 23
                        [0-18218] StaticText: ]

                  [0-24068] emphasis
                    [0-18220] StaticText: office

                  [0-24070] emphasis
                    [0-24071] link: prime minister

                  [0-24072] superscript
                    [0-24073] link: [24]
                      [0-24074] span
                        [0-18226] StaticText: [
                        [0-18227] StaticText: 24
                        [0-18228] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18229] StaticText: The prime minister still holds the office of first lord by constitutional convention,
                  [0-24077] superscript
                    [0-24078] link: [25]
                      [0-24079] span
                        [0-18230] StaticText: [
                        [0-18231] StaticText: 25
                        [0-18232] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18233] StaticText: the only exceptions being the
                  [0-24082] link: Earl of Chatham
                  [0-18235] StaticText: and the
                  [0-24083] link: Marquess of Salisbury
                  [0-18237] StaticText: .
                  [0-24084] superscript
                    [0-24085] link: [26]
                      [0-24086] span

                        [0-18239] StaticText: 26
                        [0-18240] StaticText: ]

                [0-23833] paragraph
                  [0-17978] StaticText: The
                  [0-23834] link: prime minister of the United Kingdom

                  [0-23836] link: His Majesty's Government

                  [0-17986] StaticText: .
                [0-23838] paragraph
                  [0-17987] StaticText: There is no specific date for when the office of prime minister first appeared, as the role was not created but rather evolved over time through a merger of duties.
                  [0-23839] superscript

                      [0-23841] span

                        [0-17989] StaticText: 1
                        [0-17990] StaticText: ]

                    [0-23846] link: [2]
                      [0-23847] span

                        [0-17995] StaticText: 2
                        [0-17996] StaticText: ]
                  [0-17997] StaticText: It was used in the

                      [0-23853] span

                      [0-23858] span
                        [0-18004] StaticText: [
                        [0-18005] StaticText: 4
                        [0-18006] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18007] StaticText: but did not become the official title until 1905, when
                  [0-23861] link: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
                  [0-18009] StaticText: was prime minister.
                [0-23862] paragraph
                  [0-18010] StaticText: Historians generally consider
                  [0-23863] link: Robert Walpole
                  [0-18012] StaticText: , who led the government of the
                  [0-23864] link: Kingdom of Great Britain
                  [0-18014] StaticText: for over twenty years from 1721,

                      [0-23867] span
                        [0-18015] StaticText: [
                        [0-18016] StaticText: 5
                        [0-18017] StaticText: ]
                  [0-18018] StaticText: to be the first prime minister. Walpole is also the longest-serving British prime minister by this definition.
                  [0-23870] superscript

                        [0-18019] StaticText: [
                        [0-18020] StaticText: 6

                        [0-18028] StaticText: 7

                  [0-23883] link: 1878 Treaty of Berlin

                [0-23889] paragraph
